articles.title: US lifts sanctions on daughter of military-linked Myanmar businessman
articles.summary: Delisting comes days after Trump administration reportedly reopened talks with Myanmar’s government.
articles.body:
The United States has removed sanctions on the daughter of a Myanmar businessman accused of supporting the military-installed government.

The US Department of the Treasury removed Theint Win Htet from its sanctions list on Friday, according to its website, after she sued them in July.

The decision followed a Reuters news agency report that said US President Donald Trump’s administration has opened talks with Myanmar’s government, a break from years of US policy that sanctioned the generals responsible for a coup in 2021 against Myanmar’s democratically elected government.

In January 2024, the Treasury Department under former President Joe Biden’s administration targeted the Shwe Byain Phyu Group of Companies, which was founded by Theint Win Htet’s father, Thein Win Zaw, along with his family.

The department said the company supplied fuel to the military and owned at least 20 firms with close ties to the military leadership.

Theint Win Htet originally requested her removal in a lawsuit filed against the Biden administration. That case was dismissed last year. She then filed a second complaint in July, arguing that she has no role in her father’s business.

The sanctions had blocked her US credit cards, restricted her foreign bank accounts and forced her to abandon her master’s degree at Columbia University in New York. She now lives in Thailand with her mother, who was taken off the US sanctions list last year.

Theint Win Htet’s lawyer, Washington, DC-based sanctions specialist Erich Ferrari, filed a notice with the federal court in the US capital on Friday to voluntarily dismiss the lawsuit after her delisting.

The group Justice For Myanmar has condemned the Treasury Department’s decision, saying Myanmar’s military is escalating attacks on civilians.

“It is deplorable that the US government continues to delist Myanmar cronies and their family members that provide funding for the junta’s terror,” the ‌group ‌said.

The Biden administration imposed sanctions on military officers and companies after the 2021 coup, which sparked a civil war that has killed about 100,000 people and displaced more than 3.5 million.

Washington lifted sanctions in July last year on several other Myanmar nationals and a company accused of aiding the military.

articles.title: India cracks down on ‘Cockroach’ youth protests as anger grows against Modi and election chief
articles.summary: NEW DELHI — Indian authorities deployed a sweeping security crackdown across New Delhi and detained thousands of protesters Saturday as India’s youth “Cockroach” movement sought to intensify a nationwide campaign against a contentious voter list revision that has fueled anger at Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government and election authorities.
articles.body: NEW DELHI — Indian authorities deployed a sweeping security crackdown across New Delhi and detained thousands of protesters Saturday as India’s youth “Cockroach” movement sought to intensify a nationwide campaign against a contentious voter list revision that has fueled anger at Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government and election authorities. Police moved to break up the demonstration before it could begin, intercepting demonstrators on their way to Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the heart of India’s capital, chasing off some and detaining many others. Some were dragged away before being bundled into police vehicles and taken to temporary detention centers. Several “Cockroach” movement leaders, opposition lawmakers and student activists were detained before arriving, effectively crippling the protest ahead of its start. The crackdown extended beyond the protest venue, with police stopping buses, cars and other vehicles at checkpoints on routes into the capital and searching for demonstrators. Jantar Mantar was barricaded, while anti-riot vehicles equipped with tear gas launchers were stationed along key routes. Restrictions on mobile internet and access to parts of the city added to the hurdles facing protesters. Police said Friday they had denied permission for the protest because the request was submitted late. Sambit Patra, a spokesperson for Modi’s party, dismissed the demonstrators as “anarchic elements.” “Their flop show has been completely demolished,” Patra said. The scale of the crackdown underscored the authorities’ determination to disrupt a fast-growing protest campaign that has mobilized thousands of young people, drawn opposition support and intensified scrutiny of Modi. The protests also come at a politically sensitive time, months after demonstrations led by the “Cockroach” movement over exam paper leaks forced Modi’s education minister to resign in July. Police detain leaders and tighten grip around protest site Leaders of the “Cockroach” movement Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, who were expected to be at the forefront of the protest, were detained after arriving at Delhi airport from Mumbai on Saturday. A video shared by the “Cockroach Janta Party” on X showed police boarding the aircraft and detaining the three men. “The pre-planned interception by Delhi Police aims to cripple the leadership of today’s peaceful demonstrations before they even reach the protest site,” the movement said in a statement. Loudspeakers around the protest site warned that gatherings of five or more people were banned in parts of New Delhi, as authorities imposed sweeping security restrictions rarely seen in the capital. Journalists also faced restrictions in some areas. Some protesters nevertheless broke through police cordons, chanting slogans against Modi and election authorities before being detained. “We are a democracy, yet peaceful protests are being crushed by force. Shouldn’t we fight for our rights,” said Tanya Negi, a college student who traveled from Mumbai with two friends and arrived early Saturday. “Why is Modi afraid of India’s young people?” The police response marked an extraordinary show of force in a capital where Modi’s government has repeatedly sought to contain public dissent in the past. Under Modi, authorities have often used arrests and restrictions on public gatherings to contain demonstrations, raising questions about the space for protests in the world’s largest democracy. The crackdown drew criticism from opposition leaders, who accused the government of curbing dissent. “Is there a democracy in this country? A total siege over the city. Citizens are being driven out,” opposition lawmaker John Brittas told The Associated Press. Brittas was later detained by police. India’s voter list dispute raises election fairness concerns The protests center on India’s Election Commission’s Special Intensive Revision, which the opposition says has disenfranchised millions of eligible voters. Protesters demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and an end to the change, which has removed more than 130 million names from voter lists so far. The Election Commission and the government reject allegations of voter manipulation, saying the revision is intended to eliminate duplicate and ineligible entries. The dispute has become a rallying point for opposition parties seeking to challenge Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party. Saturday’s planned demonstration follows days of protests in the Indian capital where opposition lawmakers also stepped up their campaign, with Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi being briefly detained by police. Gandhi and other opposition leaders have accused the commission of conducting the voter revision in a way that benefits Modi’s party. The opposition says voters more likely to support its parties have been disproportionately affected by the removals, while supporters of the BJP have been spared or added to the lists. The commission and the government deny the allegations. India’s youth movement broadens campaign against Modi For the “Cockroach” movement, the voter list dispute offers an opportunity to broaden its campaign. The movement began online in May and gained prominence through demonstrations, sit-ins and hunger strikes over alleged exam paper leaks. Those protests culminated in the resignation of Modi’s education minister in July, a rare political setback for a prime minister who has maintained a firm hold on national power for more than 12 years. For Modi, the protests pose a challenge midway through his third term, though their political impact remains unclear. National elections are not due until 2029, but state elections next year in BJP-ruled Uttar Pradesh, India’s most populous state, and Gujarat, Modi’s home state, will test the party’s standing.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: BJP MP Sambit Patra on Saturday termed the Cockroach Janata Party's (CJP) proposed protest at Delhi's Jantar Mantar a "flop show". The BJP MP claimed that the "anarchists" who wanted to hold Delhi "hostage" have failed."Jantar Mantar's story is not India's story. What is happening at Jantar Mantar, what you can see on TV and a few social media handles, is not India's story. India is calm and going ahead under good governance. We have been seeing that a few anarchist forces have been spreading anarchy in a corner of Delhi for the past few days. But today the anarchists have failed. The flop show of anarchist elements has completely collapsed. There was an attempt to hold India, the national capital, captive; that there be arson here, that there be violence here. But today, 'loktantra' has triumphed over bheedtantra," the BJP MP said.He alleged that the protesters had attempted to hold the country and the national capital hostage and were seeking to create violence."They were trying to hold India hostage, make the national capital hostage. They wanted violence," he said.The remarks came amid a political row over the CJP's proposed demonstration against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. articles.title: Mine water treatment by-product ochre is being used to stabilise contaminated soil at a former lead works in Chester; the site could make way for 126 new apartments
articles.summary: A long-derelict brownfield site in the heart of Chester is being prepared for a new residential development after mine water treatment by-product was
articles.body: A long-derelict brownfield site in the heart of Chester is being prepared for a new residential development after mine water treatment by-product was reused to stabilise contaminated soil.The 5,200 square metre site was historically occupied by lead works and later used as a car park. It remained undeveloped because of legacy contamination, including lead-impacted soils and asbestos-containing materials.According to the Mining Remediation Authority, ochre produced during mine water treatment is being used to manage the contamination safely on site. The approach involves mixing the iron-rich material into the ground so contaminants remain bound within the soil.Why is ochre being used at the former lead works siteThe project uses ochre from the Mining Remediation Authority’s Deerplay mine water treatment scheme in Bacup, East Lancashire. Ochre is a naturally occurring iron-rich material produced during mine water treatment. The ochre is being supplied and applied in partnership with remediation specialist Rhodar at the former lead works site in Chester.The site covers 5,200 square metres and was later used as a car park. It has remained undeveloped for years because of legacy contamination. The contaminated materials include lead-impacted soils and asbestos-containing materials.The remediation work uses ochre as part of a chemical stabilisation process. The material is mixed into the ground to bind contaminants within the soil and manage them on site.The ochre-based process helps contain lead and heavy metalsThe chemical stabilisation process is designed to limit the movement of lead and other heavy metals within contaminated soil. Ochre is mixed into the ground, where it helps bind the contaminants. This allows the contamination to be managed safely on site rather than excavated and removed.The Mining Remediation Authority has used ochre in contaminated-material treatment before. The approach was previously applied during the Mersey Gateway infrastructure project, where ochre supported the safe management of arsenic-contaminated soils at scale.At Chester, the remediation works address legacy contamination that had kept the brownfield land undeveloped. The work is intended to prepare the former lead works site for its proposed residential use while managing the contamination safely within the ground locally.How will the remediation help bring 126 new apartments to the siteThe remediation works will enable a proposed residential development of 126 new apartments at a prime city-centre location. The project is also intended to support regeneration while reducing environmental impact. Repurposing ochre gives a mine water treatment by-product a second use instead of treating it as waste.The Mining Remediation Authority said this approach supports circular-economy principles. It also reduces waste, vehicle movements and carbon emissions associated with traditional remediation approaches. The project lead, James White, said“This project demonstrates how materials produced through mine water treatment can be reused to address complex contamination challenges. Repurposing ochre to help stabilise heavy metals is reducing risk, cutting waste and supporting safe regeneration of an important city-centre site”.How is ochre being reused to help redevelop the Chester siteThe ochre being used in Chester comes from the Deerplay mine water treatment scheme in Bacup, East Lancashire. The material is collected as a by-product of the treatment process and is now being used in the remediation of contaminated land. The work connects mine water treatment with the redevelopment of a former industrial site that has remained unused for years.At Chester, the ochre-based stabilisation process means contamination can be managed on site instead of being excavated and removed. The proposed 126-apartment development can then move forward following the remediation works.The project also demonstrates the organisation’s wider use of ochre in contaminated-material treatment, including its earlier use at the Mersey Gateway infrastructure project to support management of arsenic-contaminated soils.You use AI every day. articles.title: A year after the ‘ceasefire’, Gaza’s healthcare is still collapsing
articles.summary: Continuing attacks, restrictions on medical aid and delayed evacuations are still killing Palestinians.
articles.body:
When the “ceasefire” was announced on October 10 last year, we knew how much needed repairing. For the first time in a long while, we thought we might have the breathing space to do it.

We thought medicines and equipment could arrive more regularly. Hospitals and clinics could begin to be restored. Patients could leave Gaza for treatment. Emergency medical teams could come from overseas to support Gaza’s exhausted health workers. We could finally look beyond the next crisis and plan how to care for people over the coming months and years.

Three years into the genocide, there is barely a moment to catch our breath. We’re being asked to do far more than Gaza’s devastated health system can sustain, while regular deliveries of medical supplies and equipment are still restricted and medical evacuations stalled.

People are still arriving at our clinics with traumatic injuries because Israel’s bombardment continues. More than 1,470 people have been killed since the “ceasefire” started. Even reaching a health centre can now put patients at risk. As the security situation has deteriorated, services supported by Medical Aid for Palestinians (MAP) have had to be suspended in parts of Gaza. Last month, a 65-year-old patient was killed by Israeli military quadcopter fire while seeking treatment at a MAP-supported health centre in Jabalia.

While treating new arrivals with new injuries, we are trying to look after patients whose treatment may take months or years.

Those who have lost limbs need rehabilitation, prosthetics and more surgery, but Israeli authorities heavily restrict the needed supplies. Children who survived acute malnutrition now live with anaemia and stunting, which need treatment, while people with diabetes and high blood pressure struggle to get their medicines. Cancer patients can’t get the radiotherapy they need, and people with kidney failure can’t count on regular dialysis.

Last month, a colleague of mine at MAP in Gaza lost her aunt, Iktimal. In February, Iktimal sensed something was wrong and had a biopsy, but the lab, like so many across Gaza, didn’t have the supplies to test the sample on time. It was more than a month before she learned she had cervical cancer, a disease that is usually curable when found early.

She had surgery in April, but her recovery was slow and painful, and she went on to develop kidney complications that needed specialist treatment unavailable in Gaza. Her family applied for a medical evacuation, but the process was slow, unclear, and bureaucratic. By the time Israeli authorities approved it, her condition was critical. She travelled to Egypt hoping she would finally get the care she needed, but two weeks later, she died.

Iktimal’s case is not unique. According to the World Health Organization, more than 15,000 people in Gaza are still waiting for medical evacuation; if delayed too long, many of these patients could be lost to a preventable death.

We had another tragic case a month ago: A newborn with a serious heart condition died at Assahaba Medical Complex, a hospital MAP supports. The baby needed emergency surgery that isn’t available in Gaza. The doctors knew what was needed but had no way to provide it.

Sometimes we struggle to provide treatment because even basic medical supplies are running short. Hospitals are also short on IV fluids, anaesthetics and surgical supplies. Even oxygen is in short supply.

Staff in many hospitals have to carry cylinders to a central station for refilling. Across Gaza, more than 500 patients rely on oxygen, some of them around the clock: People with cancer, pulmonary fibrosis and heart conditions, and babies and children in intensive care.

In August, the Palestinian Ministry of Health warned that 22 of Gaza’s 34 oxygen stations had stopped working, and only four of 30 machines used to fill oxygen cylinders were still running.

The stations that still function could fail soon. Israeli authorities continue to block the spare parts needed to repair them, classifying them as “dual-use” items. For similar reasons, Gaza has no working MRI machine, and only one or two CT scanners serve about two million people.

Doctors are sometimes left to make decisions without the scans, tests or medicines they would normally rely on.

A cancer that could have been caught early becomes harder to treat. An injury that could have healed with rehabilitation becomes a permanent disability. A child who needed proper food and treatment can be left with chronic malnutrition, stunting and developmental difficulties that may last a lifetime.

We were told the “ceasefire” would give people in Gaza time to heal and rebuild. It hasn’t. The restrictions that stood between Iktimal and her diagnosis, her treatment and her evacuation are still in place, and her story is one of thousands across Gaza in the past year.

Every delay has a cost. Every week a medicine is held back, a scan can’t be done, a patient is refused exit, someone’s condition passes the point where it can be treated.

Iktimal ran out of time. Right now, thousands of people in Gaza are running out of time, too.

articles.title: How drones are hunting fires hidden beneath the Cairngorms
articles.summary: Dramatic flames from the huge Cairngorms wildfire in July have disappeared - but hot spots can continue to burn beneath the earth.
articles.body:
It is 06:00 and I'm meeting drone pilot Pete Short for a dawn patrol in the Cairngorms National Park.

It is a job he has been doing for almost three months, since a huge wildfire tore through this landscape in July.

The flames which swept across the hillsides are gone. From where we are standing, there is little to suggest there is still a fire here at all.

But that is exactly what we have come to find.

After a bumpy drive into the woodland, Pete launches a thermal drone into the early morning sky.

I am given a job too: keeping the aircraft in sight while he studies the images being sent back to his screen.

"Every week I hope that I find none," he tells me. "On the last thermal flight I did we found eight."

"We might have something here," Pete says, as a white glow appears on the thermal image beneath a tree.

Three months after the fire first ignited, heat is still being detected beneath the ground.

We make our way towards the coordinates identified by the drone, and at first, there is almost nothing to see.

The soil is warm. A rock Pete picks up from the ground is, too.

Nearby, after scraping away a thin layer of earth, smoke begins to rise.

"It's really now cooking away," Pete says.

"Without the thermal technology we would be totally blind to this."

The wildfire began in the middle of July and burned across about 3,300 hectares – 33 sq km – of land, according to the Cairngorms National Park Authority.

At the height of the emergency, five experienced drone pilots were brought together to provide aerial information to the agencies fighting the fire.

Pete describes it as one of the most challenging environments he has ever flown in, with "multiple walls of flame", personnel and vehicles moving around the site and helicopters operating overhead.

The dramatic flames have disappeared, but hot spots can continue to burn beneath the earth.

Each one found by the drones is reported to the land manager. They send teams who can dig into the ground and douse it with water.

For Ben Jones, senior site manager for the RSPB at Abernethy, knowing exactly where to send those teams has been crucial.

"We've been fighting this fire for over two months now and obviously we've got limited resources in terms of the number of people we have and we can't send everybody out everywhere all the time," he says.

"So we really need to know where these specific hot spots are - where we should be sending people - so that they can be as efficient as possible."

And despite the arrival of colder, wetter weather, the remaining fires cannot simply be ignored.

"Each of these hot spots has got the potential to reignite a larger fire," Ben says.

Walking through the forest, the scale of what happened is almost haunting.

Tree trunks are blackened and charred. The acrid smell of fire still hangs around. Large areas of the forest floor have been scorched.

But look closely and there are splashes of colour.

Green shoots are emerging. Fungi is growing. I even spot a small yellow flower shooting up from the blackened ground.

Dr Sarah Henshall, head of conservation at the Cairngorms National Park Authority, says it is too early to know the full ecological impact of the fire.

"Some of that will be incredibly quick, some of it will take years, decades, or even beyond our lifetime," she says.

"It will recover, but we just don't know what that's going to look like yet."

And the drones that helped during the fire - and are still searching for what remains of it - are being given another job.

Pete is programming them to repeatedly fly exactly the same routes over the damaged landscape.

Using predetermined waypoints, photographs and video can be taken from the same positions month after month and year after year, allowing conservationists to build up a picture of how the landscape changes.

"This standard drone route will have exactly the same route flown month by month, year by year and visually it's going to give us some amazing information about how it's recovering," Sarah says.

There could be another role for the tech too - spotting future fires before they have a chance to spread.

Pete believes getting a view above the tree canopy quickly could prove critical.

"It's those moments before a wildfire gets out of control that could be critical to stopping it before it gets out of hand," he says.

Back on the ground, our patrol has found another hot spot.

Again, there is almost nothing visible from a distance. But guided by the drone, we find the precise spot.

Beneath a thin layer of earth, it is hot and the smoke becomes obvious after we stoke the soil.

Another location to report. Another fire for the ground teams to extinguish.

Above us, the forest is already showing its first signs of life but below our feet, the last of the fire is still burning.

articles.title: Suspect killed after 13 kindergarteners taken hostage, beaten in Brazil
articles.summary: Man spreads flammable liquid in a room with 13 children while holding a lighter as police try to negotiate.
articles.body:
Brazilian police have rescued 13 children who had been taken hostage at a kindergarten in the southern city of Curitiba after killing the suspect, who threatened to set fire to the building, according to officials.

At least one of the children was wounded in Friday’s incident, the commander of the military police special forces unit in Parana state, Alexandre Lopes Dias, told reporters without elaborating on who or what injured the child.

Parana police spokesperson Leticia Martins told journalists outside the kindergarten that the suspect jumped the gate on Friday, broke into a classroom and held 13 children hostage.

He then spread a flammable substance in the room and held a lighter in his hand. He was carrying a knife and also what was initially believed to be a firearm, but later was found to be fake.

“Our negotiating teams were in place but saw no alternative but to neutralise him,” said Martins, who did not specify whether the suspect had expressed a specific reason for his actions.

The incident took place in the neighbourhood of Sao Braz in Curitiba, a city of 1.8 million residents located 400km (250 miles) south of Sao Paulo.

Lopes Dias told reporters the suspect was identified as a man who suffered from schizophrenia, but he did not reveal the man’s identity or how he was killed.

“During the entire negotiation, he stayed with all the children around him and one on his lap,” the police official said.

Talks lasted up to three hours. The children became agitated, and the attacker started hitting them, Lopes Dias told reporters.

“Once we realised that the kids were becoming increasingly upset and that the attacker started assaulting them physically, we opted for a tactical intervention to avoid a greater problem,” he explained.

Local media showed footage of tearful parents outside the school waiting for information as the negotiations between the suspect and police were ongoing. Minutes after what local media described as flash bangs, officers emerged carrying some of the children outside.

“We entered the classroom using a very tactical approach with little risk for the children,” Lopes Dias added.

Curitiba Mayor Eduardo Pimentel wrote on Instagram: “The 13 children are alive and safe! After anguishing and tense moments, this is the news we were all waiting for.”

Brazil in recent years has experienced multiple attacks on schools. In April 2023, a man killed four children with an axe at a day care in Blumenau, also in southern Brazil.

Curitiba City Hall said in a statement that the children and school staffers would receive psychological support.

articles.title: 'Wrongfully confined': CJP legal head moves court against police for detention during lawyers' stir
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Ratna Singh, legal affairs head of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), has moved a Delhi court seeking registration of an FIR against police
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Ratna Singh, legal affairs head of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), has moved a Delhi court seeking registration of an FIR against police personnel. She has filed it alleging that police personnel confined her and prevented her from joining a lawyers’ protest against chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over the conduct of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR). In her application filed on Saturday, Singh also sought a status report from the police on the alleged incident.Singh filed the application before chief metropolitan magistrate Abhinav Pandey at Saket district court. She has sought directions for registration of an FIR against the police personnel allegedly involved. She has also asked the court to call for a status report from the concerned authorities.According to the application, Singh is a practising advocate. She was proceeding towards the Supreme Court with two fellow advocates to participate in a protest by lawyers against the CEC and the SIR exercise.The plea alleges that Singh was later sitting in a car with advocate Tara Narula outside her residence when she was prevented from moving. Two cars allegedly blocked her vehicle from the front and rear. Police personnel remained outside the car, preventing her from proceeding further.Singh has alleged that the police personnel did not explain the legal basis for restricting her movement, despite her asking them to do so. She has described the alleged incident as wrongful restraint and confinement.The application also refers to a police call made in connection with the incident and provides details of the call. Singh has raised concerns over her safety and liberty. She has argued that the circumstances warrant urgent intervention by the court.Singh has further stated that a video of the alleged incident may be examined by the court. In her plea, she has claimed that her life and liberty are under threat. She has sought legal action against the personnel allegedly involved in restraining her.The application comes amid protests by members of the legal fraternity against the chief election commissioner and the SIR exercise. The proposed demonstration has brought attention to the right of lawyers to assemble and express their views, as well as the role of police authorities in regulating protests and maintaining law and order.Lawyers detained near Supreme CourtOn Saturday, a group of lawyers holding a protest march against the chief election commissioner and the SIR exercise were detained by personnel of the Delhi Police and the Central Reserve Police Force near the Supreme Court.The detentions prompted the Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA) to urgently approach Chief Justice of India Surya Kant. The association wrote to the CJI about several advocates being detained while peacefully protesting outside the Supreme Court.According to the SCBA's communication, the detained lawyers were taken to Yamuna Sports Complex. The association raised concerns over the detention and sought the CJI's intervention.Following the SCBA's urgent communication, the CJI conveyed to the authorities that the detained lawyers should be released.The detention of the lawyers and Singh's allegations have brought the police action surrounding the protest into focus. While the lawyers were detained near the Supreme Court, Singh has alleged that police personnel separately prevented her from joining the demonstration.CJP legal head seeks judicial interventionRatna Singh's application seeks judicial intervention over the alleged restriction on her movement. She has asked the court to direct the registration of an FIR against the police personnel allegedly involved in the incident.She has also sought a status report from the concerned authorities to place details of the incident before the court. Her plea refers to the alleged blocking of her vehicle, the presence of police personnel outside it, and the absence of an explanation for the restriction despite her asking for one.Singh has contended that the alleged restraint requires examination by the competent authorities. She has cited concerns over her liberty and personal safety in seeking the court's intervention.The allegations in the application are yet to be established. The plea seeks an FIR and a police status report in connection with the alleged incident.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: You’d never guess the crazy things cash welfare paid for. Nebraska is shutting that down
articles.summary: Nebraska and Florida are blocking cash welfare spending on alcohol, porn, tattoos and more, following Trump administration guidance on TANF reform.
articles.body: Beer. Liquor. Cigarettes. Porn. This isn’t just a list of things that can be bad for you. This is a list of things that Americans are buying with cash welfare, thanks to a massive loophole in federal law. Thankfully, states are finally taking action to prevent this abuse and protect taxpayers, with strong guidance from the Trump administration. It’s an overlooked — but important — new front in the ongoing War on Fraud. DOJ THREATENS TO CUT BILLIONS IN WELFARE FUNDING FROM STATES FOR FAILING TO REPORT ILLEGAL MIGRANTS The latest state to close this loophole is Nebraska. On Oct. 9, Republican Gov. Jim Pillen directed the state to stop recipients of cash welfare from spending money on items like tobacco, porn, tattoos, psychic and fortune-telling services, luxury watches and much more. Going forward, if you receive money under the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) program in Nebraska, you cannot spend the money on things the taxpayer shouldn’t be funding in the first place. Americans may be forgiven for wondering why people in Nebraska — or anywhere else — were ever able to buy these things with cash welfare. After all, most people assume that government assistance is only supposed to fund specific things that families need. Cash welfare in particular is explicitly designed to help low-income families "achieve economic security and stability." So, how did cigarettes and smut enter the picture? PRO-LIFE VS SOCIALISM: GOP LAWMAKERS DIVIDED OVER CONTROVERSIAL GUARANTEED INCOME PROGRAMS It’s true that federal rules stop you from spending cash welfare at places like liquor stores. But you can still buy alcohol at plenty of other places, such as grocery stores. Similarly, you can’t spend cash welfare at casinos or strip clubs, but you can still gamble or buy pornography in plenty of other places. This loophole has existed for roughly 30 years, since TANF began — and it’s so large, it’s laughable. Did lawmakers not realize that alcohol isn’t just sold at the corner store? Do our nation’s leaders not know that "adult entertainment" is available outside of seedy clubs? WHITE HOUSE PUSHES 'WATERSHED' FRAUD-FIGHTING REFORM IN CONGRESS AS VANCE CONVENES TASK FORCE These are far from the only non-essential — and deeply questionable — things that cash welfare is funding. Taxpayers are also able to pay for things like concert tickets, streaming subscriptions, tattoos and luxury services like spa treatments. It’s enough to make you wonder: When Congress created cash welfare, did it put any meaningful restrictions on how the money could be used? Unfortunately, closing this loophole in one fell swoop would require another act of Congress. But thankfully, the Trump administration has issued guidance explaining how states can close this loophole, one by one. States can’t change federal requirements for cash welfare. But they can ask the federal government to approve stronger requirements on a state-by-state basis, which explains the sudden and welcome progress. Before Nebraska, Florida took the first meaningful action to stop this abuse. In August, Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis announced that he was blocking cash welfare from being spent on tobacco products, drugs, porn, tattoos, video games, fortune-telling services, and a slew of other obviously non-essential goods and services. The Trump administration quickly approved the Florida plan, which DeSantis rightly said will protect "Floridians who genuinely need assistance" while also guarding taxpayers from fraud and abuse. What are other state leaders waiting for? CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION It’s shocking that any state has allowed such blatant abuse of the taxpayer’s generosity for so long. Perhaps they’ve been waiting for Congress to act, but given the dysfunction in D.C., that was always a long shot. Regardless, now is the time for governors to act. The easiest thing to do is to follow Florida and Nebraska’s lead and simply amend their state plans for cash welfare. Governors could also work with state lawmakers if they want to ensure more permanent reforms, while holding retailers accountable for circumventing restrictions. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Bottom line: Every state must close this cash welfare loophole. No one should be using the taxpayer’s money to buy pre-mixed cocktails and porn. articles.title: Ohio dog park shooting over Trump argument could end with two self-defense claims, or none: legal expert
articles.summary: Both men in the Ohio dog park shootout over Donald Trump could claim self-defense or neither could, a legal expert says, creating a rare puzzle.
articles.body: A shootout sparked by an argument over President Donald Trump at an Ohio dog park could end with a jury finding that both men acted in self-defense, or that neither did, a legal expert told Fox News Digital. Emmanuel "Mike" Mathews, 81, is charged with felonious assault for shooting David Mattai, 55, on April 21 at Centerville Mills Park in Bainbridge Township, according to authorities. Mathews has pleaded not guilty. Case Western Reserve University law professor Michael Benza said that under Ohio law, defendants lose the right to claim self-defense if they helped ignite the confrontation that led to the shooting. VIDEO SHOWS MOMENTS BEFORE ARMY VETERAN WAS FATALLY SHOT IN WALMART PARKING LOT DISPUTE Since both men allegedly took part in the escalation, he said, the case presents a unique legal puzzle. "They could both be found at fault, which means neither of them would get self-defense," Benza told Fox News Digital. Since self-defense relies heavily on subjective fear and perceived danger, Benza said, "It's also possible both get self-defense." Competing accounts Mathews' attorney, Ian Friedman, said the encounter began as a verbal argument, which turned physical in the park before ending in gunfire in the park’s parking lot. "Mr. Mathews was attempting to leave," Friedman told Fox News Digital. "He was attempting to keep himself safe." Friedman said it started when Mattai, who overheard Mathews talking to an eyewitness about Trump, disagreed with Mathews' view that Trump is one of the country's greatest presidents. Bainbridge Township Patrolman Friedrich Kaufmann testified at Mathews’ May 5 preliminary hearing at Chardon Municipal Court that following that initial verbal altercation, Mattai drove away, then returned to the park about five minutes later. FLORIDA MEN WIELDING HATCHET AND MACHETE CLASH IN PUBLIX PARKING LOT, POLICE SAY Mathews was still sitting at a picnic table with his dog when Mattai returned. Mathews gathered his belongings and began walking toward his vehicle, but after crossing to the other side of a park fence, an exchange of insults between the pair caused a physical confrontation. GUN-WIELDING COUPLE IN VIRAL BLM STANDOFF GOT FIREPOWER — AND 'A VOICE' — BACK AFTER LEGAL SAGA Friedman said that Mattai grabbed Mathews by the hair and pulled him into the fence. Mathews also reported being headbutted. Mattai denied the headbutt allegation, but Friedman said an injury below Mathews' eye supports that account. Following the physical altercation, both men retreated toward their vehicles after witness Jamie Jedlinsky, 70, reportedly stepped in to diffuse the situation. OHIO MAN CONVICTED AFTER TRYING TO SHOOT EX-WIFE AT POINT-BLANK RANGE INSIDE RESTAURANT IN CHILLING VIDEO Mathews got into his vehicle and allegedly placed a .45-caliber gun on his dashboard, when Mattai, who stood in the parking area after loading his dog in his vehicle, saw the weapon. The men allegedly exchanged words before Mathews fired once. Mattai retrieved a 9mm Taurus handgun from inside his Hyundai, then fired six shots "almost contemporaneously" near Mathews' head and body, according to Friedman. "We believe that Mattai was turning to retrieve his gun and coming back to aim at Mathews when the bullet struck the lower right portion of his back," Friedman added. Mathews was not injured in the gunfire exchange, but Mattai's return fire hit Mathews' vehicle at least four times. Mattai previously told The New York Times that he did not physically touch Mathews after seeing Mathews’ weapon, and fired back in fear of his own safety. Mattai’s wife, Sally Mattai, told the Times that her husband almost died after suffering a severe gunshot wound to his lower back that damaged his spine and required two separate emergency surgeries. Mattai's attorney, Ryan Fisher, said he believes public opinions have convoluted the case and created confusion. "There are a great deal of differing opinions of what went on in the dog park that day," Fisher told Fox News Digital. Fisher's response did not address the defense's claims about the gun or the timing of the shots. Geauga County Sheriff's Office deputies arrested Mattai Aug. 5. He’s currently facing misdemeanor charges of assault and disorderly conduct. 'You can't be the first one to draw the gun' Benza said introducing a firearm changes the legal footing of a physical scuffle, but he emphasized that the order of events greatly matter. "You go from OK, we're hitting each other... physically, punches are being thrown. Now you've pulled a weapon. You have now escalated this fight, which then justifies me escalating my response by then pulling my own gun and defending myself," he said. "But you can't be the first one to draw the gun." Ohio law removes the duty to retreat when someone is lawfully in a location. Friedman said that since Mathews was legally allowed to be at the park, he had no obligation to flee. "He certainly had no duty to retreat," Friedman said. "Had he done anything different from what he did do in those seconds, he may not be here to talk about it today." Political challenges Friedman said although the verbal argument began over politics, his client acted out of fear for his safety, not political retaliation. "This was never about a political dispute for Mr. Mathews," he said. Benza, however, said the county’s politics could potentially complicate seating a jury, regardless of why the incident happened. "In Geauga County, where this happened, it is a very Republican-dominated county," Benza said. "The one defendant may be concerned that he will end up with jurors who are very pro-Republican or pro-Trump, which would create his concerns about a fair jury." "The other defendant may want a pro-Trump jury because they would be so, well, he got what he deserved or something to that effect." SEND US A TIP Now, the case may come down to a jury deciding whether Mathews had a genuine, reasonable fear for his life when he is accused of shooting Mattai. GOT A TIP? Friedman predicted the evidence would show Mathews should never have been arrested, while Fisher said the case is "going to have to be flushed out by the jury in the upcoming trial." Mathews’ trial is scheduled to begin Feb. 16, at the Geauga County Court of Common Pleas. GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL If convicted, he could face a minimum sentence of five years and a maximum potential sentence of 15 years in an Ohio state prison, due to combined penalties of a second-degree felony assault charge and a mandatory firearm specification. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Mattai is scheduled for a pretrial hearing Oct. 28, at the Chardon Municipal Court. He told the Times that he is "willing to plead guilty or no contest," if it means no jail time.

articles.title: Inside the protest playbook to vilify Israel on 'global day of action'
articles.summary: Global Alliance for Palestine distributed a detailed playbook urging groups to shut down city squares and blockade corporate hubs across continents.
articles.body: WASHINGTON, D.C. – As demonstrators, including the headline-grabbing CodePink agitators, descend on the nation's capital late Saturday afternoon for a "coordinated global day of action" against Israel, they will join a worldwide wave of marches and planned disruptions that may appear to be unfolding independently. In Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, on Friday, anti-Israel demonstrators carried signs deploying emotionally charged language against Israel, including one featuring a Palestinian flag and a bloodied hand with the message, "STOP GENOCIDE." Nearby, two women carrying mock machine guns flanked a cardboard image of a handcuffed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu with a noose around his neck. But a Fox News Digital investigation has found that, long before the first demonstrators gathered, the messages for the protest's "communications framing" and transnational action plan had already been written, the banners designed, the tactics circulated and the media strategy laid out to "turn public outrage into collective leverage." The campaign documents reveal that coalition organizers instructed participating groups to direct protesters to "shut down city squares," "encircle government buildings" and "blockade complicit corporate hubs." The document declares, "This is not a symbolic march and not a routine protest." Fox News Digital identified 179 organizations in the coalition, while an interactive Google Map published by the network lists 322 events scheduled across three days through Sunday. They include a rally on an "Intifada Trail" in Saint John, New Brunswick, Canada, a protest in Bangladesh by the "Bangladesh Intifada Youth Collection" and actions in South Africa by "Social Intifada." All three use "intifada," a term associated with Palestinian uprisings against Israel, including periods marked by deadly terrorist attacks. Activists describe the term as a call for resistance. The global coordination illustrates how contemporary protest movements combine international leadership, local activist networks, standardized visual branding, emotionally charged messaging and traditional news outreach into a single mobilization infrastructure in which professional political organizing amplifies the sincerely held convictions of individual demonstrators. LAWMAKERS THROW OUT 'TROJAN HORSE' ACTIVISTS THEY SAY ARE ENGAGED IN AMERICAN SUBVERSION Among the participating organizations is CodePink, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that has received $1.33 million from Neville Roy Singham, a Shanghai-based tech tycoon who has funneled $278 million into a network of nonprofits under scrutiny by the House Ways and Means Committee and its chairman, Rep. Jason Smith, over allegations that some operate as "Trojan horses" and proxies for the Chinese Communist Party and other malign foreign interests. CodePink and other organizations under scrutiny have denied wrongdoing. Two days ago, CodePink co-founder Medea Benjamin and D.C. coordinator Olivia DiNucci dispatched a letter to members, directing them to join the "Feminist Contingent" at the Library of Congress for the "global day of action." "And don't forget to WEAR PINK!" they noted. The network's connections were also visible last week, when CodePink co-founder Jodie Evans, who married Singham in 2017, joined an anti-Israel protest in New York City, marching behind a band of activists from Revolutionary Communists of America as they chanted, "Long live the intifada." Evans told Fox News Digital Singham supports CodePink's efforts and the "amazing work" nonprofits are doing to "stand up when violent things are happening." Taken together, the documents reveal a coordinated protest and influence campaign spanning continents, combining accusations of Israeli "genocide," attacks on the news media, workplace and university walkouts, blockades, political lobbying and carefully orchestrated publicity. A review of the planning documents for the global protests reveals the machinery behind the wave of anti-Israel demonstrations across continents as not only a protest campaign but a psychological operation: a common playbook combining strategic accusations of Israeli "genocide," attacks on the news media, workplace and university walkouts, blockades, political lobbying and coordinated publicity. At the center of the international mobilization are three organizations identified in the campaign documents: the "Global Alliance for the Palestinian territories," launched in July 2025 in London as a "truly international popular front for Palestinian liberation"; the "Anti-Apartheid Movement for Palestine"; and the "Global Coalition to End the Occupation of Palestine." An online directory displays 179 organizational logos from participating groups worldwide. Fox News Digital extracted the names from the logos and built a database of the coalition. The same pattern of coordinated organizing has emerged in another international protest movement: the so-called "student protests" rolling through France. A separate Fox News Digital investigation identified a network of 50 organizations coordinating and amplifying those demonstrations. Only 15 were classified as youth- or student-led groups, while the remaining 35 included communist organizations, labor groups, political organizations and professional protest coordinators. Organizers supplied participating groups with campaign materials, coordination and strategic support to "turn public outrage into collective leverage." In an August "Launch Statement," the alliance laid out a strategy to synchronize student demonstrations, workplace actions, rallies and civil disobedience across Asia, the Americas, Europe, Africa and the Middle East. The stated objective wasn't simply to organize demonstrations, but to add Israel's war in Gaza to the international media agenda, turning separate protests into a coordinated communications effort intended to shape what audiences around the world see, hear and think about the conflict. But the most revealing aspect of the operation may be its stated objective: shaping what the world sees, hears and thinks about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. In a "Launch Statement" in August, the alliance declared that the demonstrations are intended to return Israel's military campaign against Palestinians to the international media agenda. The campaign materials describe a strategy of synchronizing protests across continents, connecting student demonstrations, workplace actions, rallies and civil disobedience from Asia to the Americas, Europe, Africa and the Middle East. The result is a coordinated communications campaign designed to transform demonstrations organized by separate groups into the political impact of a single international mobilization. ISRAEL, JEWS TARGETED WORLDWIDE AS WELL-FUNDED LEFTIST, ISLAMIST GROUPS JOIN FOR ‘NAKBA 78’ PROTESTS Weeks before the demonstrations, the alliance had already prepared a collection of campaign posters in seven languages – English, Arabic, Turkish, Finnish, French, Portuguese and Spanish. They supplied graphics for a large street banner carrying carefully selected slogans, along with protest-sign designs from folders marked "HANDHELD PLACARDS" and "STREET DEMANDS." One of the downloadable images is a poster with the message "GAZA GENOCIDE" next to graphics of barbed wire and watermelon, both symbols of Palestinian "resistance" against Israel. In Malaysia, a woman wearing a black-and-white Palestinian keffiyeh raised her fist while holding a printed version of the watermelon-and-barbed-wire placard], with the organizers' branding in smaller letters on her sign: "GLOBAL ALLIANCE FOR PALESTINE." Behind her, other women carried the same sign and other signs featuring additional graphics from the same campaign materials. Other placards held by protesters in Malaysia yesterday, read, "HUMANITY IS NOT A CRIME" and "STOP THE GENOCIDE WAR!" Another downloadable sign, carried in Malaysia, reads: "LET GAZA LIVE!" The campaign's "Communications Framing" employs familiar techniques of political persuasion: repetition, emotional imagery, collective identity, moral urgency and the portrayal of inaction as complicity. The materials offer a window into the battle for public attention that increasingly accompanies international conflicts. One poster declares, "You cannot erase a homeland." Another commands, "End the genocide. Defend the land." A third combines an image of a child with the message, "Defend the land. Protect its children." Another repeats the words "Silence normalises" across the background before presenting the word "genocide" in oversized red lettering. But the campaign's internal messaging guidance goes further, prescribing accusations against Israel and the news media in a section called "Slogans & Hashtags," with "Call to Action & Core Street Demands." Among its recommended slogans is the blunt declaration: "Israel Kills. The Media Justifies." Another declares, "1,100 Days of Israeli Genocide — The Killing Continues." Yet another calls for action under the message, "1,100 Days — From Every Street, One Demand: End Genocide, End Occupation." Together, the slogans strategically combine accusations of "genocide" with demands for political action, while claiming the media "justifies" Israel's conduct. In its "Concept Paper," the alliance describes Israel's actions as a "war of extermination" and calls for countries to stop providing weapons to the Israeli state. The same document instructs participating organizations in its "Communications Framing" to use language that is "disciplined, credible, urgent and impossible to ignore." It also directs organizers to portray "institutional silence" as part of the problem and public mobilization as necessary to confront what the alliance calls continuing complicity. The objective isn't simply to communicate a political position, but to encourage audiences to emotionally identify with a movement and participate in its activities. The campaign presents its allegations of "genocide" and other violations of international law as established claims. On Friday, South African human rights lawyer Navi Pillay received the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her work, which included arguing that Israel has committed a "genocide" against Palestinians. Israel disputes the "genocide" accusation. ANTI-ISRAEL GROUPS RALLY ACROSS US ON OCTOBER 7 ANNIVERSARY, CHANTING 'LONG LIVE THE INTIFADA' The organizing documents go beyond encouraging supporters to attend demonstrations. Instead, organizers describe a campaign intended to "interrupt business-as-usual" and organize "high-visibility rallies, marches, picket lines, sit-ins and peaceful blockades" at "civic sites, government offices, financial hubs and corporate locations" that its organizers have "identified as complicit in sustaining or normalising Israeli violence." They also recommend synchronized "workplace, campus and creative interruptions," including "silent walkouts," banner drops, nighttime projections, street theater, "die-ins" and "other highly visible public actions that interrupt normal routines and make the political demand impossible to ignore." A detailed logistical plan urges organizations to "allocate funds," arrange transportation and establish "legal, stewarding, and participant support." ISRAELI PM NETANYAHU ARGUES PUBLIC OPINION SHIFT ON ISRAEL 'CORRELATES ALMOST 100%' TO SOCIAL MEDIA The organizing documents go beyond encouraging supporters to attend demonstrations. The campaign's organizational structure brings together prominent political figures with longstanding backgrounds in international politics and anti-Israel activism in Europe, the Middle East, Africa and Asia. A press release for the protests identifies seven members of the international steering committee, including: former British Labour Party leader Jeremy Corbyn, who joined a coalition supporting the Communist Party of Cuba; pro-communist former Greek finance minister Yanis Varoufakis; former Sinn Féin leader Gerry Adams; Palestinian political leader Mustafa Barghouti; former South African government minister Ronnie Kasrils; Indian activist Varsha Gandikota-Nellutla; and Italian politician Angelo Bonelli. Anas Altikriti serves as secretary-general. Jessica Breakey, the campaign's public relations officer, didn't respond to a request for comment. Beyond the streets, the alliance's strategy documents lay out a plan to convert the demonstrations' visibility into "sustained political pressure" on lawmakers and government institutions. In a separate advocacy document, organizers urge participating groups to mobilize protesters to write lawmakers, submit coordinated institutional letters and arrange meetings with elected representatives. The campaign calls for "immediate, total arms embargoes" and "comprehensive state sanctions" against Israel for alleged violations of international law. It also urges governments to suspend preferential trade agreements and institutional partnerships associated with Israeli policies. The alliance demands an end to what it calls Israel's "genocide and occupation," without specifying whether its reference to occupation encompasses Gaza, the West Bank or the entire State of Israel. The distinction takes on particular significance amid chants of "from the river to the sea" at anti-Israel demonstrations. Organizers encourage participating groups to use "targeted, template-driven letters" and "digital briefing toolkits" to support "localised political campaigning," adapting them to their national political systems. The documents provide direct instructions that participating organizations issue local press releases, distribute "ready-made social-media toolkits," share "graphics across digital channels" and hold briefing sessions to "ensure clear, aligned messaging ahead of the weekend." articles.title: DEPROGRAMMED: How a man radicalized by the Taliban became a counterterrorism force saving lives from extremism
articles.summary: Mubin Shaikh reveals how the Taliban radicalized him in Pakistan and how marriage and 9/11 sparked his deradicalization and counter-terrorism career.
articles.body: Mubin Shaikh, a former Jihadist radicalized by the Taliban, details the radicalization process that enamored him with extremist ideology, before he snapped out of those views to become a counter-terrorism specialist for the United States and Canada. "The biggest indicator [of radicalization is] what we call pathway to violence behaviors. So, doing reconnaissance on a target, looking up, you know, where's the local synagogue? Where's the local mosque?" Shaikh told Fox News Digital. "It's very important for parents, educators and others to be aware of these signs so that they can possibly prevent the next attack," he continued. AMERICAN YOUTH RADICALIZED ONLINE, BUSTED IN SUSPECTED TERROR PLOTS AFTER HATING COUNTRY ON SOCIAL MEDIA Shaikh’s introduction to radicalization began after a house party, where his uncle "guilt tripped" him into thinking the party was the "most heinous thing possible" he could’ve done that "dishonored" his family. "That’s what made me tell myself, I need to get religious, and that is what would start my radicalization," he continued. That incident prompted his travels to India, Syria and Pakistan, where he was radicalized by the Taliban. SHE WAS MARRIED TO AN AL QAEDA MEMBER. NOW ONE WOMAN IS FIGHTING THE TERRORISM SHE SAW UP CLOSE "The city that I was sent to in Pakistan was called Quetta and was and is a Taliban stronghold… I had a chance encounter with the Taliban who basically impressed upon me that the only way for me to really be successful in this world and the next world was to be a militant, was to fight in jihad," he added. "Me, [as] this young man looking for a sense of meaning, belonging [and] identity, these guys gave me what I thought I was looking for - and I became a supporter of their mentality," Shaikh continued. A few years later Shaikh got married — a reality he says started to clear the smoke around his extremist views. MUSLIM JAIL GANGS SAID TO FORCE CONVERSIONS ON PRISONERS IN UK: 'JIHADIST TRAINING CAMPS’ "The abstract conversations around theology and geopolitics yielded to the very real reality in front of me of having a wife and the idea that I could have a future, I could start a family, and so that became more important for me in my life. And that was basically addressing intimacy needs that every human being has. And so my interest in the extremist world started to wane a bit," he said. September 11th, 2001 would later become the biggest single catalyst in deradicalizing Shaikh. The worst terrorist attack in American history prompted him to travel to Syria, and research Islamic studies in depth. "I would spend two years there studying Arabic and Islamic studies and would go through this period of de-radicalization," he continued. MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD-LINKED NETWORKS EMBEDDED ACROSS CANADIAN INSTITUTIONS, NEW REPORT ALLEGES When he returned to Canada, "the first Canadian had been arrested on terrorism charges after the newly minted post-9-11 anti-terror legislation" - Momin Khawaja - a fellow classmate and peer of Shaikh from Quran school during his childhood. Shaikh saw reference to the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (CSIS) and reached out to them, thinking Khawaja’s accusal a mistake. Once they confirmed his classmate’s arrest and spoke more to Shaikh, CSIS recruited him as an undercover operative in counterterrorism efforts. "I was already online, looking at the extremism that was out there… and by 2012, started to see the rise of ISIS in real time. It was at this time that the US government reached out to me and said, 'Hey, can you help us out with what's coming?' And so from 2012 to 2020, I participated and I supported the coalition against ISIS in various anti-ISIS activities and operations," he continued. HEZBOLLAH GROOMS CHILDREN FOR MARTYRDOM THROUGH ITS SCOUT MOVEMENT, REPORT CLAIMS Shaikh works now as an exit peer specialist for Parents for Peace, a nonprofit fighting radicalization and extremism by intervening with individuals before it’s too late, most of whom "overwhelmingly are juveniles" under 18. "What gives me hope in countering extremism is really seeing how people turn out after they've left extremist ideologies. It's like a night-and-day difference. And when they come to see the mistake that they were making, when they come to see the pathway that it was leading them towards and seeing that they have left that, their lives get better, their personal situation gets better," he continued. "To see parents, you know, have their kid back again — that's what it's all about," Shaikh said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

articles.title: UCLA vs Oregon betting preview and spread analysis as undefeated squad eyes a major upset
articles.summary: No. 21 UCLA's ground-heavy rushing attack faces Oregon's 39th-ranked run defense in a college football playoff-shaping conference showdown.
articles.body: Each week we get a little bit closer to the games that matter most. The College Football Playoffs are closer than you probably realize and we are essentially at the halfway mark for the year. We will still have the conference championships and a few of the lower-level bowl games, and plenty of great matchups in between. One of those great matchups happens today as UCLA takes on Oregon. UCLA comes into the game as the 21st-ranked team in the nation. The Bruins are 4-0 for the season and currently 2-0 in conference play. In Week 1, UCLA took on Cal on the road and was able to win 45-24. Then in Week 2, the Bruins hosted San Diego State University, winning 28-10. The offense didn’t really get rolling, but their defense was good enough to get the stop. The Bruins faced Purdue in Week 3, and they got the offense back on track with a 52-38 victory. Then on the road against Maryland, they had their best game of the season, winning 54-3. Last week was a bye week, giving them a chance to prepare for this one. Most of their work has been done on the ground, as Nico Iamaleava has just 820 passing yards and four touchdown passes. They will need him to be elite against Oregon if they want to pull off an upset. The Oregon Ducks are 3-1 for the season and back up to 13th in the nation. It has not been a smooth ride to start the season with a couple of narrow victories and one upset. Week 1, the team hosted Boise State, and won 34-27, but this wasn’t exactly a comfortable game. The Ducks finally got the stops needed in the fourth quarter and the game-winning score. In Week 2, the Ducks couldn’t find a way to escape the loss. They faced Oklahoma State on the road and lost 39-31. It was one of those classic games where they were teetering toward a loss and then finally lost this one. In order for UCLA to pull off the upset, it needs to make this a grind-it-out type game. The running attack has been very good. The Bruins have run the ball 60 more times than they’ve thrown it this season, so clearly they know their strength. Oregon ranks 39th in the nation against the run. Oregon will look to use a balance of both the run and pass to get a win. However, it does feel like this still might not be enough to cover the spread. I don’t have much confidence in either of the quarterbacks. I lean to the over, though, as both teams should find some holes and put up at least 25 points each. I’m going to take the points with UCLA. Oregon just doesn’t look that good this season. articles.title: What has Trump’s Board of Peace achieved in a year since Gaza ‘ceasefire’?
articles.summary: Analysts say board has ‘failed’ in its attempts to secure lasting peace in Gaza.
articles.body:
It has been one year since United States President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace (BoP) brokered a “ceasefire” aimed at eventually ending Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza.

However, rather than receiving relief and a chance to rebuild, Palestinians in the enclave continue to face attacks and be uprooted as Israeli forces have expanded control within the territory.

Trump first proposed the BoP in September 2025, saying it would stabilise Gaza and ensure lasting peace.

In November, a United Nations Security Council resolution recognised the board as a “transitional administration” in Gaza.

But what has the board achieved? Here’s what we know:

The BoP’s mission was laid out in Trump’s 20-point Gaza peace plan , as was the “ceasefire” between Israel and Hamas. The ceasefire began on October 10, 2025.

The plan envisioned steps for each side to take that could eventually create a “credible pathway” to Palestinian statehood.

It required Israeli forces to withdraw to about 50 percent of the Gaza Strip and cease aerial and artillery bombardments. It also required Israel to release 250 Palestinian prisoners and another 1,700 people jailed from Gaza since October 7, 2023, the day that Hamas led attacks into southern Israel and Israel began the war. The plan proposed reopening border crossings to allow much-needed aid into Gaza.

The peace plan required Hamas to release all Israeli captives. It also proposed a later phase in which the group would disarm and its members would be granted amnesty or a safe exit from Gaza.

The peace plan established the BoP as a transitional governing body until the Palestinian Authority, which governs parts of the occupied West Bank, could take over.

An International Stabilization Force (ISF), led by the US, was supposed to take over security in Gaza from withdrawing Israeli forces, the plan stated. It also proposed the reconstruction and redevelopment of Gaza, whose people, it said, “have suffered enough”.

In February, the BoP’s members, who each joined in exchange for a $1bn annual fee, met in Washington, DC, for its first summit, at which member states pledged $7bn in funding although aid agencies said reconstructing Gaza would cost closer to $70bn.

On the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York last month, the BoP also unveiled a 66-project recovery plan worth $2.4bn.

The BoP’s achievements are tied to the success of the Gaza peace plan.

Under that, Hamas has released all 168 living captives and Israel has freed Palestinian prisoners.

Hamas has also announced the dissolution of its government in the Gaza Strip although Israel has dismissed that as a “stunt”.

Other goals under the peace plan have been only partially met.

Governance has been hampered. While a National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), meant to act as the governing authority in Gaza, was founded, Israel has not granted it entry into the Strip. The NCAG reports directly to the board and is led by Chief Commissioner Ali Shaath and other Palestinian technocrats. It operates from Cairo. Israel has not stated why the committee is not permitted to enter Gaza.

Aid remains restricted. About 227 aid trucks enter the Strip daily when 600 trucks were supposed to, according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) hunger monitor.

Israel has classified thousands of basic items, such as tents and essential equipment like ventilators, as “dual use” items, which means they have military and civilian applications, and has restricted their flow into the Strip. About 1.4 million Palestinians – or most of Gaza’s more than 2 million people – will suffer hunger until at least December, the IPC has noted. That is 200,000 more than those who faced hunger in May, suggesting a significantly deteriorating situation.

Observers argued that the BoP has entirely failed to secure the “ceasefire” as Israeli attacks have continued almost daily on the Strip.

Since October 10, 2025, more than 1,400 Palestinians, mostly women and children, have been killed. In the three years since the war began, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed, and thousands more are missing and presumed dead under the rubble.

Israel says its continuing attacks target Hamas members, but the group vehemently denies the claims.

Israel also now occupies about 60 percent of the Strip, more than the 50 percent agreed in Trump’s peace plan. The “Yellow Line”, which demarcates the area of Gaza under Israeli occupation, has been pushed farther into the Strip, causing further displacement and squeezing Gaza’s population into an ever-shrinking area. Palestinians unknowingly crossing the “Yellow Line” have been shot dead.

In December, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said the army “will never fully leave” the Strip.

Mohamad Elmasry at the Doha Institute of Graduate Studies told Al Jazeera that Israel is simply continuing a broader policy of “ethnic cleansing” in Gaza and the occupied West Bank. “They are making life miserable,” he said, adding: “This is all by design.”

Consequently, the BoP has also failed to ensure Hamas disarms so phase two of the peace plan could begin.

Although Hamas has agreed to hand its weapons over to the NCAG, it rejects the “disarmament” clause because Israel has not ceased its attacks or withdrawn from the Strip as agreed. At the same time, Israel has said it will not move forward with the plan if Hamas does not disarm, leaving the two sides in a standoff.

Meanwhile, no stabilisation force has been deployed. Six countries – Indonesia, Morocco, Kazakhstan, Albania, Kosovo and Uganda – have so far committed personnel to form a security force of 20,000 soldiers and 12,000 police headed by the US military’s Central Command (CENTCOM).

There has been no meaningful reconstruction in Gaza. Palestinians continue to live in tent camps infested with rodents and insects with little to shield them from intense heat, or rain.

The Trump administration and BoP have echoed Israel’s rejection of the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees, or UNRWA, which has long provided lifesaving humanitarian aid, education, development programmes and social services in Gaza and employs about 11,000 Palestinians.

The BoP said last month that it will not work with UNRWA, essentially sidelining the agency.

A BoP official told The Associated Press news agency that UNRWA could continue working in Gaza if its programmes were deemed relevant but the agency’s “days are over”.

In June, the UN General Assembly voted overwhelmingly to extend UNRWA’s mandate until 2029. The BoP itself is mandated to oversee the peace process until December 2027 when its progress will be reviewed for possible renewal by the UN.

Analysts and rights groups have raised concerns that the BoP could take over all aspects of Gaza’s rebuilding. Countries too, including France and other European nations, have called out any attempts to replace the UN in the Strip.

But Elmasry said no country is willing to take action. “There are a lot of international actors that do not want to cross the US,” he said. That essentially leaves the fate of more than 2 million Palestinians to Trump, he added.

Ultimately, the BoP has “failed”, said Simon Mabon, a professor at Lancaster University.

“The failure to implement its own plan to end the Gaza conflict demonstrates its impotence and the inability to ensure that Israel and, to a lesser extent, Hamas, remain bound by their own commitments [and] has allowed the genocide to continue,” he concluded.

articles.title: Why Alabama, with its high-powered offense, could be the team to finally challenge unbeaten Georgia
articles.summary: College Football Week 6 features a massive SEC showdown as Keelon Russell and Alabama host second-ranked Georgia in a clash of unbeaten powers.
articles.body: College Football Week 6 is here, and with it comes one of the biggest games of the season. It seems like the two schools square off each year, and it is always a great game. That’s what happens when two of the best teams in the country and two of the top programs in college football meet, and tonight we have Georgia taking on Alabama. This season, Georgia comes into the game as the second-ranked team in the country. They are a few years removed from being the best defense in the league. Now the team seems to have a better offense than defense. Still, the team hasn’t been bad on the defensive side of the ball, either. The Bulldogs haven’t allowed more than 20 points in a game this season, but they also haven’t faced anyone that impressive. In Week 1, the Bulldogs played Tennessee State and won by 60 points. In Week 2, they won by 50. Then in Week 3, they at least faced some more difficult opponents. They beat Arkansas on the road, but by "only" 28 points. Oklahoma came to face them in Week 4, and they won by 28 in this game as well. Last week, they played against Vanderbilt, and they won by 24 points. At no point in this season have they been tested or had to face a tough team. FIVE IMPORTANT COLLEGE FOOTBALL QUESTIONS THAT WILL BE ANSWERED AFTER THIS WEEKEND'S SLATE The Alabama Crimson Tide brings a 5-0 record of their own, and a rank of sixth in the nation. It has taken a while for the program to look good, but Alabama has been pretty solid through the first five weeks of the season. It isn’t like the Tide have faced anyone overly difficult outside of last week, but the team has looked good on offense, like it will be hard for anyone to stop. When these two get together, it seems like something always happens that is memorable. Georgia rocked Alabama in the SEC Championship Game last season, 28-7, but Alabama won the previous three meetings between the two teams. This game is in Tuscaloosa, so Alabama does get the edge. I like what I’ve seen out of Keelon Russell and think he can lead the Tide to victory. I’m going to take Alabama to win the game at -122.
