articles.title: Delhi protests: Over 3,000 detained as CJP stir against CEC triggers political face-off - top developments
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Delhi Police detained over 3,000 people across the national capital on Saturday as the Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP) proposed protest against
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi Police detained over 3,000 people across the national capital on Saturday as the Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP) proposed protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar was met with heavy security deployment and restrictions. The demonstration was called over allegations of voter-list manipulation during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) and changes relating to Form 6, used for voter registration.Several protesters, activists, lawyers and opposition leaders were detained as they attempted to reach Jantar Mantar, where Delhi Police had denied permission for the gathering.The detentions also triggered sharp exchanges between the Opposition and the BJP, with Congress leaders accusing the government of suppressing dissent, while the ruling party defended the restrictions and criticised the protest.Over 3,000 detained, heavy security across DelhiDelhi Police detained more than 3,000 people during the day as demonstrators attempted to reach Jantar Mantar, officials said, as quoted by PTI. CJP leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were detained inside their aircraft upon arrival from Mumbai, while YouTuber Dhruv Rathee was picked up from his Gurugram residence.Other political leaders, activists, lawyers and protesters were also detained at several locations across the capital including Mamata Banerjee, Arvind Kejriwal. Police deployed thousands of personnel, erected barricades and imposed traffic restrictions to prevent large gatherings in central Delhi. Several metro stations were closed, while authorities also imposed mobile internet restrictions in parts of the city.However, despite roadblocks and metro closures, a few protesters travelled for hours or walked long distances to reach the protest site. Despite barricades, traffic diversions and metro closures, a few protesters found their way to central Delhi on Saturday, travelling for hours or walking long distances to reach the protest site. “We are the youth of this country. If we don't come, who will?” said Meer, who rode a scooter for two hours from Sarita Vihar, a squoted by PTI. Another protester, Lakhan, questioned the response to people raising their voices, saying, “The public is hungry. Answer their questions.”Delhi Police had denied permission for the protest, citing procedural requirements, public safety and traffic management concerns. The CJP had called the demonstration to demand Kumar’s resignation over allegations concerning the SIR exercise.In a separate development, police informed Dipke about the death of his 85-year-old paternal grandmother, Savitribai Shankarrao Dipke, in Maharashtra’s Hingoli district. According to a police statement, he was also offered possible assistance to travel to his hometown on humanitarian grounds to attend her last rites.3 former CMs detainedArvind Kejriwal, Mamta Banerjee, Pinarayi Vijayan were among the several detained by Delhi Police amid anti-SIR protests. Former West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee was detained along with Trinamool Congress MPs while attempting to reach Jantar Mantar. She later said she had begun a dharna at Dwarka North police station with five party MPs, alleging they had been taken away in a prison van and driven around for two hours despite complying with police instructions. “We were kidnapped and driven around in a prison van for two hours,” Banerjee wrote on X. She also said she would remain in Delhi and join the INDIA bloc’s march on Monday, adding, “It is a super emergency.”Read more: Mamata alleges Delhi Police 'kidnapped' her, driven around in prison van for 2 hrsKerala chief minister Pinarayi Vijayan was detained during the protest, prompting condemnation from CPM leaders. In a Facebook post after being taken into custody, Vijayan accused the NDA government of turning Delhi into an “open prison” and using armed police and paramilitary forces to suppress demonstrations. He alleged that the Centre was attempting to turn India into a “police state” and said the struggle to protect the Constitution and voting rights would continue.Meanwhile, former Delhi chief minister Arvind Kejriwal was detained outside his residence while attempting to join the protest. Before his detention, he accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi of acting out of fear of the CJP demonstration. “This is worse than the Emergency. It's official… We are living under an absolute dictatorship ruled by Modi,” he wrote on X. He also alleged that the BJP had won elections through “vote chori” and said, “Gyanesh must go, but so must Modi.”Read more: Former CMs Mamata Banerjee, Pinarayi Vijayan and Arvind Kejriwal among opposition leaders detained from DelhiPolice personnel injured in stone-peltingTwo Delhi Police personnel were injured after protesters allegedly pelted stones at security personnel near Akashwani Bhawan on Imtiaz Ali Marg. Around 25 to 30 protesters allegedly jumped barricades and threw stones at security personnel around noon, following which some were detained.In a separate confrontation near Baba Kharak Singh Marg in Connaught Place, a police head constable said a scuffle broke out as personnel tried to disperse protesters and that a stone struck his shoe. Inspector Vivek Kumar said a group of protesters advanced towards a small police contingent before reinforcements arrived. Stones were also pelted at a bus carrying detained protesters in the Jhandewalan area, officials said. Police continued detaining demonstrators attempting to reach Jantar Mantar, where permission for the protest had been denied. About 500 people had been detained at the time of the initial report, while subsequent police figures put the overall number detained across Delhi at over 3,000.Congress accuses government of suppressing dissentThe leader of opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi took aim at PM Modi, home minister Amit Shah and RSS. "I’ve been fighting Narendra Modi and the RSS for over a decade now. I understand them like you would understand your opponent - inside out, like the back of my hand. The core characteristic of these people is cowardice. Narendra Modi, Amit Shah, Mohan Bhagwat, Gyanesh Kumar and Ajit Doval, the villains of this story, are slowly finding the space closing around them. We are closing that space. Mr. Modi, do whatever you want. Call out all the police: 10,000, 20,000, 50,000, whatever you want. Arrest all the leaders. Arrest all the young people. Arrest us all," he said on X.Priyanka Gandhi also criticised the mass detentions saying, "First they rough up 254 MPs and detain them completely illegally, infringing on their basic constitutional rights; they do the same to other protestors from Opposition parties. Then they lay siege to the national capital, barricading it and sealing it on all sides, stopping trains and metros, cutting the internet and placing check posts all over. They bash up and detain young men and women exercising their constitutional right to protest."Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge criticised the Modi government over the detentions, saying it had turned the “Mother of Democracy” into a “Muzzled Democracy”.In a post on X, Kharge said students, lawyers, journalists, social activists, farm union leaders, YouTubers and content creators questioning the government were being detained. He asserted that the Congress and the united Opposition would continue to fight the government and defend democracy, the Constitution and citizens’ fundamental rights.Congress leader Shashi Tharoor also criticised the restrictions, questioning why roads leading to Jantar Mantar had been placed out of bounds despite the site being designated for public demonstrations.Former Rajasthan chief minister Ashok Gehlot accused the BJP of attempting to discredit the Opposition for raising questions about the electoral process. He defended the right to protest and criticised internet restrictions and detentions during demonstrations.Meanwhile, Congress general secretary KC Venugopal announced that the Congress and the INDIA bloc would hold a major protest in Delhi on Monday, October 12, as part of their campaign over voting rights and electoral reforms.BJP defends action, accuses Opposition of promoting unrestBJP MP Ravi Shankar Prasad criticised the Opposition’s protests, asserting that the country would be "governed by Parliament and not the streets". He said the protests amounted to attempts to create anarchy and argued that the BJP’s electoral victories in Assam, Nandigram and Puducherry demonstrated the strength of Indian democracy.Prasad said the BJP was not opposed to protests but accused the Opposition of using street demonstrations in response to electoral defeats while saying "CJP is shadow boxing for AAP".BJP national spokesperson Sambit Patra also defended the government, saying the events at Jantar Mantar did not reflect the situation across the country. He alleged that certain forces had attempted to create unrest in Delhi but had failed.The BJP’s response came amid continued criticism from opposition parties over the denial of permission for the CJP demonstration and the detention of protesters seeking to reach Jantar Mantar.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Celebrity chef says people have Southern food all wrong, shares what her family ate
articles.summary: Tiffany Derry challenges Southern food stereotypes, pointing to her Louisiana farm roots and family meals built around fresh vegetables, peas and greens.
articles.body: Southern food may have a reputation for being heavy and unhealthy, but celebrity chef Tiffany Derry says that stereotype misses a big part of what's traditionally been served on tables across the South. "I think a lot of times that criticism comes from folks who don't actually understand the South," Derry told Fox News Digital. The Texas-born chef and restaurateur, who competed on "Top Chef" and recently became a judge on "MasterChef," pointed to her own family's Louisiana roots as an example. 'MASTERCHEF' FINALIST SAYS BUSY FAMILIES ARE LOSING SOMETHING MORE IMPORTANT THAN HOME-COOKED MEALS "We had a farm," she said. "I ate from the farm very much." Derry said fresh vegetables were a routine part of meals growing up — long before "farm-to-table" became a restaurant buzzword. "It wasn't this farm-to-table thing. It was what you did," she said. Neighbors would share what they grew, while meals featured relatively small amounts of protein alongside rice, peas, vegetables and beans, Derry recalled. DOLLY PARTON'S FAVORITE SOUTHERN DISHES, FROM CHICKEN AND DUMPLINGS TO BANANA PUDDING She said foods commonly associated with Southern cooking today don't tell the entire story. "It's important to not just tell the story of the country cooking where we talk about mac and cheese and we talk about biscuits and biscuits and gravy," Derry said. "People don't really understand where food comes from." Those heavier dishes represented "such a very small amount of the cooking" and weren't "everyday" foods in her experience. Cooking was also a family affair. Derry said her grandmother had 11 children and she has more than 50 cousins. As a child, Derry helped prepare greens, peas and green beans. After 27 years in the restaurant industry, however, Derry believes she's seeing renewed interest in cooking at home. She recalled a period when Americans seemed to be cooking less and some people "just didn't really know how to cook." Now, she said, younger generations are seeking out recipes on TikTok, entertaining at home and even embracing bread-making. "I love the fact that people are interested in sourdough. Like, are you kidding me?" Derry said. "People are back making bread." Derry sees the evolution firsthand on "MasterChef," where home cooks can progress to producing food that looks as though it came from professional chefs. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS She also noted that some younger cooks learned differently from previous generations. "So many of their parents didn't really cook," Derry said. "And so they learned on their own, and they learned through watching and through chefs and TV and reading books and magazines and all of that." Derry spoke with Fox News Digital while promoting a partnership with Tostitos and the brand's new Chunky Guacamole for football season. She said tailgating food has undergone its own transformation, ranging from traditional burgers to Kobe beef sliders and increasingly elaborate spreads made for Instagram. articles.title: BROADCAST BIAS: Media skip Mamdani’s ‘genocide’ comment but love him bashing ICE
articles.summary: From CBS Mornings to NPR, Oct. 7 anniversary coverage revealed troubling media bias patterns in how they cover Israel, Gaza and Benjamin Netanyahu.
articles.body: The third anniversary of the merciless slaughter of Israelis, as well as Americans, on Oct. 7 drew some solemn media coverage remembering the attack. If there’s a day that the news should display a pro-Israel bias, it would be on this anniversary. But on this subject, our broadcast networks have a disturbing tendency toward "both-sidesism." That’s the clunky word they use when they complain that it’s not moral to present pro-Trump and anti-Trump views as morally or factually equivalent. The best journalism should tilt toward the "right side" of our world. That generally means the liberal side in their view. On Oct. 7, "CBS Mornings" anchor Gayle King was Exhibit A in moral equivalence: "three years ago today, Hamas unleashed a horrific attack on civilians in southern Israel, killing 1,200 people and taking another 250 hostage. Israel responded with an all-out military offensive in Gaza that killed more than 70,000 people, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry run by Hamas." NEW YORK TIMES ISSUES CORRECTION, DELETES LINE QUESTIONING IF ISRAELIS WERE VICTIMS OF OCT 7 TERROR ATTACK The impression that leaves is that Israel is 60 times worse than Hamas. The first problem here is using a terrorist group for your statistics. The left-wing media do this without blinking. Naturally, Hamas does not distinguish between its combatant casualties and civilian deaths, and the networks rarely note that Hamas routinely surrounds its soldiers and weapons with civilians with the aim of causing maximum civilian casualties. The other bias bubbling up on Oct. 7 was the bias against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whom journalists dislike almost as much as President Donald Trump. CLINTON, BUSH RECEIVED MULTIPLE WARNINGS ON BIN LADEN HIJACK PLOTS BEFORE 9/11, DECLASSIFIED FILES SHOW ABC’s "Good Morning America" had just 75 seconds on the anniversary, which mostly focused on allegations that Netanyahu was warned in advance these attacks were coming. President George W. Bush faced this kind of partisan attack after 9/11, that there were warnings of an al-Qaeda attack on America. Foreign correspondent James Longman summarized: "One claim, that the UAE warned the prime minister a week and a half before it happened, but those warnings were not passed on. Another that the head of Egyptian intelligence came to Israel to warn about Hamas preparing something. There’s also outrage about how long it took for security forces to respond. Now, Benjamin Netanyahu has called all this lies and a smear campaign." BROADCAST BIAS: FROM FLYDUBAI TO BENGHAZI, THE MEDIA STRUGGLE TO KEEP POLITICS OUT OF TERRORISM On the homepage of National Public Radio on the morning of Oct. 7, their top headline announced: "3 years on, Israelis grapple with reports Netanyahu was warned before Oct. 7 attacks." NPR’s reporters in Israel dramatically began: "Israelis are reeling from new revelations in Israeli and U.S. media that the country had been repeatedly warned by its regional allies that Hamas was planning to attack." They cited four anonymous sources with "direct knowledge." But we have no "direct knowledge" of their identities or motivations. NPR added that Netanyahu has denied all this, calling the reports "fake news" and filing a defamation lawsuit last week against Israeli news outlets that published them. They surely see that as the Trump playbook. NEW YORK TIMES ACCUSED OF FRAMING MUSLIMS AS TRUE VICTIMS OF 9/11 IN ANNIVERSARY COVERAGE The evening newscasts on ABC, CBS, and NBC didn’t use any Hamas body counts. But ABC disposed of the subject in a cursory 13 seconds. The other two were somber stories marking the dark day. CBS anchor Tony Dokoupil added: "In the years since, more antisemitic violence has followed. Targeting kids at Temple Israel in Michigan, a young couple outside the Israeli Embassy in Washington, and a Hanukkah celebration on Australia's Bondi Beach." The "PBS News Hour" devoted 13 minutes to the anniversary, much of it with Jonathan Dekel-Chen and Jaser Abu Moussa, two men who lost family members on opposite sides of the war, trying to reject hate. They were appearing at the 92nd Street Y in New York that night. MAMDANI DOUBLES DOWN ON ANTI-ISRAEL OCT 7 STATEMENT AFTER BACKLASH None of the networks focused on the controversy in New York, where Muslim Democrat Mayor Zohran Mamdani issued an Oct. 7 statement that mourned the "unthinkable loss" of that day, and then shifted into his traditional loathing of Israel: "The suffering did not begin nor end that day. It instead continued through the Israeli government’s devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza." The impression that leaves is that Israel is 60 times worse than Hamas. The first problem here is using a terrorist group for your statistics. The left-wing media do this without blinking. The mayor added to the insult by showing up that night at a candlelight vigil in Union Square, where anti-Israel protesters, some of them with Hamas and Hezbollah flags, booed and yelled at him with jeers like, "Zohran, you can’t hide, we charge you with genocide." ANTI-ISRAEL GROUPS RALLY ACROSS US ON OCTOBER 7 ANNIVERSARY, CHANTING 'LONG LIVE THE INTIFADA' Then, Mamdani suddenly appeared on the broadcast networks after the anniversary, when the subject changed to an ICE shooting during an enforcement action in New York. On Friday, Oct. 9’s "Today" show, reporter Erin McLaughlin touted "the mayor now calling for ICE to leave New York City." Mamdani’s soundbite was "We know that ICE is rotten to its core." These are not words he would use for Hamas. articles.title: Philadelphia police officers shot 15 times combined in ambush attack, suspect found hiding in tree
articles.summary: Two Philadelphia police officers were ambushed and shot multiple times on North 52nd Street. Kevin Bethel says one officer was hit 12 times.
articles.body: Two Philadelphia police officers are in the hospital after being shot early Saturday while responding to a call in the western part of the city. One officer, a 40-year-old who has two children, was shot three times, Philadelphia Police Commissioner Kevin Bethel said during a news conference. The other officer, a 33-year-old who has five children, was shot 12 times, Bethel said. CONNECTICUT POLICE OFFICERS SHOT, SUSPECT KILLED AFTER ATTEMPTED ARREST SPARKS HECTIC CHASE "I am so damn proud of the men and women who serve in this department. Consistently, they go into danger, and they give their lives for this job," Bethel told reporters. "And so we ask for those prayers, and we ask for you to support our men and women out there, and what they give for this profession." Just after 12:20 a.m., the officers were dispatched to 140 North 52nd Street following a report of a man with a gun on a porch, Bethel said. About 30 minutes later, the officers arrived at the address and came under "significant gunfire" once they were on the porch. Shortly after shots were fired, Bethel said additional officers and a SWAT team found the original responding officers on the porch with gunshot wounds. CHICAGO OFFICERS WOUNDED IN TRAFFIC STOP SHOOTOUT AS HOLIDAY WEEKEND LEAVES 3 DEAD, 16 INJURED The suspect fired at two additional officers, Bethel said, but the SWAT team was able to locate the man in a tree and take him into custody. The officers who were shot were taken to Penn Presbyterian Medical Center for surgery. Their conditions are not clear. "We are praying now that our officers make it through this terrible situation," Bethel said. The suspect reportedly ambushed the officers by running down an alley and shooting at them, local outlet WPVI reported. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The suspect, whose name has not yet been released, was found with two handguns and a shotgun, Bethel said. One of the handguns belonged to one of the officers who had been shot. The Philadelphia Police Department did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

articles.title: Why is US turning to Russia for diesel despite sanctions?
articles.summary: President Donald Trump’s deal with Putin comes amid surging fuel prices and looming US midterm elections.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump says he has agreed a deal to release stocks of diesel fuel from Russia to try to ease high fuel costs in the US before November’s midterm elections.

However analysts told Al Jazeera that the deal will likely have little effect on easing the global energy crisis while European countries could refuse to buy from Russia altogether.

The agreement comes despite years of sanctions on Russia over its war on Ukraine, the latest of which were announced last month by the US and specifically targeted buyers of Russian oil .

On Friday night, Trump announced on social media that after a “highly successful discussion” with Russian President Vladimir Putin, it had been agreed that Russia would “immediately” supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel fuel to the US and global marketplace.

Another 500,000 tonnes would be released in November, and a further 1 million tonnes sometime after that, Trump said. He added that, based on the current condition of its diesel refineries, Russia would then deliver another 3 million tonnes of diesel.

Trump claimed that this move, along with what he described as “total control” by the US of the Strait of Hormuz, would bring down diesel prices in the US and the rest of the world.

“Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority,” he wrote in a post on his Truth Social platform.

Trump later thanked Putin for the deal, telling reporters outside the White House on Friday: “To be honest, we have massive amounts of oil coming into our country, and it’s diesel which is what we want.”

Putin said in a statement on Friday that Russia “confirmed its willingness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US market and global markets at large”.

Global fuel prices have surged as a result of both the US-Israel war on Iran and Russia’s war on Ukraine. Tehran has largely closed off the Strait of Hormuz, through which 20 percent of the world’s oil and gas supplies had been shipped in peacetime, since the US and Israel first launched strikes on Iran in February.

The recent attack on Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline , another key oil export route from the Gulf, as well as attacks by Yemen’s Houthis around the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandeb strait have compounded supply disruptions.

Meanwhile, oil refineries and energy and port facilities have come under heavy attack in both Russia and Ukraine.

Global fuel inventories have plummeted, and diesel prices reached record highs in both the US and Europe in September.

Last week, the Group of Seven countries agreed to release 100 million barrels of emergency reserves of diesel and crude oil after a US pressure campaign on the European Union in which the Trump administration threatened a US ban on its diesel exports.

Hamad Hussain, a climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, told Al Jazeera last week that the impact of the G7 release “would be short-lived given that this is just a temporary solution to the supply crunch”.

How has the diesel crisis affected the US?

Surging diesel prices in the US saw the national average rise to a record $6.52 a gallon (3.79 litres) in September, more than twice the price from a year earlier. The national average is currently $6.20, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA).

The US is the world’s largest diesel exporter. Its inventories have fallen sharply since the Iran war began and remain below normal levels despite refiners increasing their output.

In September, US lawmakers and Trump floated restricting diesel exports in a bid to lower consumer costs. Trump also called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt attacks on diesel fuel targets, accusing him of causing a shortage after Ukraine ramped up its strikes on Russia’s oil industry this year, aiming to disrupt its energy industry, which it uses to fund its war effort. Trump did not single Russia out for similar treatment over its attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.

Trump is particularly concerned about bringing down the price of diesel before the US midterm elections. The Iran war is already deeply unpopular and many small-business owners in his MAGA (Make America Great Again) support base rely on diesel being affordable.

Consumers are feeling the effects of rising prices as diesel is used by truckers to transport food and products and by farmers operating machinery. The latest Pew Research Center polling indicated that the economy is the most important issue for 84 percent of registered voters.

States that voted for Trump and typically support candidates from his Republican Party, like Iowa and Kansas, are now seen as battlegrounds in the November 3 elections, putting Trump under pressure to avoid a Republican defeat.

What does this mean for US sanctions on Russian oil?

The US banned imports of Russian oil and gas in 2022 under the Biden administration in response to the invasion of Ukraine in February that year.

A sweeping Russian sanctions law passed in Congress last month and signed by Trump also targets countries that buy Russian oil and gas. The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 expanded existing sanctions and aimed to pressure Putin by targeting officials, banks and shadow tankers that facilitate the Russian energy trade.

It also gave Trump the power to impose 100 percent tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil and natural gas.

After Trump’s announcement on Friday, the US Department of the Treasury said the Office of Foreign Assets Control was “immediately issuing a temporary general license to allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market”.

Isn’t Russia having a fuel crisis of its own?

Yes, it is, giving analysts reason to doubt that Russia will be able to release as much diesel as Trump is promising.

Neil Atkinson, former head of the International Energy Agency’s oil industry and markets division, told Al Jazeera that he is sceptical about Russia being able to do this.

“In the very short term, it’s very hard to see how Russia can deliver the volumes that are talked about in the deal other than at the expense of its domestic market,” he said.

Russia was previously the world’s second-largest diesel exporter after the US. But Russian diesel and gas exports in the third quarter of this year were at 190,000 barrels per day compared with 690,000 barrels per day in the second quarter and 850,000 barrels per day in the first quarter, explained Michelle Wiese Bockmann, a maritime intelligence analyst with the shipping analytics company Windward, citing data from the commodities tracker Vortexa.

Russia, therefore, banned diesel exports in July in a bid to meet domestic demand and in late September expanded the ban until the end of October.

Ukraine’s attacks on Russian energy facilities have also contributed to the fuel crisis in Russia. Putin has admitted that 1 percent of Russia’s gross domestic product has been affected by Ukrainian attacks.

Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence said its air strikes have destroyed more than half of Russia’s oil refining capacity. In July, it also struck hundreds of Russian shadow fleet tankers in the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea, affecting the delivery of gas to Crimea, which Russia annexed in 2014.

Bockmann told Al Jazeera that Russian domestic shortages were “so acute that over the third quarter for the first time we saw Russia import gasoline and diesel and gas oil”.

She added that “as recently as this week”, a ship carrying diesel and gas oil arrived in the port of Vysotsk.

Last week, Russia said it would consider a partial lifting of diesel export restrictions in the case of overproduction. Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told the Russian parliament that the domestic market was balanced and “if diesel production exceeds domestic demand, we will consider partially reopening exports.”

Russia typically produces double the diesel needed to meet its domestic needs, according to the International Energy Agency. It has different standards of diesel suitable for different temperatures. Its summer-grade diesel for temperatures over 0 degrees Celsius (32 degrees Fahrenheit) may be released to make way for the winter and Arctic grades needed domestically in the coming months.

Trump’s announcement came as US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, were meeting with Ukrainian officials and European negotiators in Miami, Florida, to discuss ending the Russia-Ukraine war, now in its fifth year.

Zelenskyy reacted to the announcement, saying it was “a weak decision by strong partners”.

He said the deal “plays into Russia’s hands,- allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer”.

Can Russian diesel ease the pressure on global prices?

On Friday, Putin said he was “convinced [the agreement] will have a positive impact on the entire global economy”.

The Russian president also noted that “an agreement was reaffirmed to maintain personal contacts between the presidents of the two countries and to continue cooperation across their respective administrations, security services and agencies.”

Analysts said the agreement will do little to address the global energy crisis, however.

Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG Group, told Al Jazeera that the Trump-Putin deal to release Russian diesel is a short-term solution and “another classic Trump deal”.

“Announce an ‘agreement’ with an unpleasant dictator with impressive headline numbers and no certainty that any of the objectives will be achieved,” he said. “Even if some of the diesel does make it out of Russia, it is only a short-term solution given the globe’s daily consumption of diesel is around 30 million barrels,” which is roughly the total amount that could be released under the outlines of the deal that Trump announced.

Bockmann also told Al Jazeera that it is unclear how much impact releasing Russian diesel will have on reducing prices and global shortages.

“I’m not sure how effective the issuing of the general licence will be in allowing volumes to be imported at levels that are going to impact the domestic price of diesel in the US,” she said.

Atkinson said the volumes announced by Trump – even if Russia could manage to provide them – “don’t really move the needle very much” on prices because the US uses about 3.7 million barrels of diesel a day.

There are also indications that European countries may not even buy diesel from Russia.

“It’s very hard to see how a European government could, in all morality, buy oil from Russia when the whole point of the last four years is that Europe has been trying to wean itself off Russian oil and gas supplies as soon as practical,” Atkinson said.
